An agentic pre-flight check.

⚠ some-other-package@1.0.2 — published 4 hours ago Blocked: fails the 7-day cooldown policy.

Your agent installs whatever package name sounds right. OSS IQ runs first: does this exist, is it a typosquat, was it published this morning, is anyone still maintaining it. Hallucinated and freshly-published names get stopped at the gate, not in production — ossiq add is a quality gate in front of npm install and uv add.

Built for the axis nobody else covers.

Audit tools grade the past — which CVEs are already in your tree. Dependabot grades nothing and opens a pull request for everything. OSS IQ grades the move forward: what it costs to stay current, what breaks if you upgrade, and whether a package is worth depending on at all.

10/10

The same answer every time.

Run the same upgrade ten times unassisted and the agent settles on two different dependency trees. Both pass the tests, so no pass/fail benchmark will ever catch it. With OSS IQ, ten runs out of ten converged on one answer — and the cost spread narrowed from 4.5× to 1.6×.

Two commands, two answers.

One for the project you already have. One for the package your agent is about to add.

 blast radius & upgrade plan
# no install — Python toolchain, or Node
$ uvx ossiq status
$ npx @ossiq/cli status

# solver-backed plan, transitive cascade included
$ ossiq plan --production

# rewrite the manifest, roll back on failure
$ ossiq apply
 safety check before install
# inspect drift, CVEs and health first
$ ossiq info requests

✓ 2.31.0 recommended · no CVEs · maintained
⚠ latest 2.32.0 — single maintainer, bus factor

# quality-gated install of the right version
$ ossiq add requests

# wire it into Claude Code, Codex or Copilot
$ ossiq install skills

Held to the standard it measures.

A tool that forecasts supply-chain risk in other people's dependencies has no business being sloppy about its own. Every artifact OSS IQ publishes is verifiable before you run it.

SLSA Build L3
Every published artifact carries signed SLSA v1.2 Build Level 3 provenance — PyPI wheels, GitHub Release binaries, and the npm packages.
Builds sign under a workflow identity isolated from the one that publishes, so provenance can't be forged by anyone who can only edit the release plumbing. Verify with gh attestation verify.
No standing creds
PyPI and npm both publish through OIDC Trusted Publishing.
There is no long-lived registry token to steal. Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a full commit SHA.
Hashed & offline
Dependencies are locked with a SHA-256 per artifact and installed with uv sync --locked. Packaging makes no network calls.
A CycloneDX 1.5 SBOM is generated from the lockfile and attested alongside each artifact.

The Docker image installs from PyPI and sits outside this chain — verify the wheel instead. Full detail and the exact verification commands: SECURITY.md.

Cost, time and consistency figures come from our Round 3 agent benchmark, 28 September 2026: 60 sessions across two projects and three delivery modes, ten seeds each, paired by seed with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Headline numbers are the static-report delivery mode; the MCP server saves 29% on cost and 33% on time. Every arm reached 100% verified-correct results on these fixtures — including the unassisted control — so we make no claim that OSS IQ improves correctness. Two six-dependency fixtures are not production repositories; larger graphs and real repositories are the next tests.
